strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: understanding how vision-language models resolve conflicts between internal parametric knowledge and counterfactual visual evidence.

WHOOPS-AHA! provides a controlled token-level benchmark with anomalous images, paired prompts, and factual/counterfactual continuation sets. The construction prompts, public model implementations, GPU budget, and planned code/dataset release support reproducibility.

The analysis combines observational localization with causal testing: Logit Lens across blocks and heads, modality-specific attention analysis, direct attention-head intervention, and image-patch ablation, supplemented by random-head and random-patch controls.

The main intervention effects are large and consistent across LLaVA-NeXT-7b and Gemma3-12b. Reweighting the selected heads shifts factual accuracy from 22% to 74% and from 18% to 83%, respectively, while reversing the intervention reduces factual accuracy and randomly selected heads have little effect.

Attention from the identified conflict-resolution heads localizes visually anomalous regions more effectively than gradient magnitude and random-patch ablation under the pixel-removal evaluation. Qualitative examples, such as the rainbow bearskin hat and fruit on the operating table, are intuitive and semantically aligned.
The paper is generally clearly written, and the limitations section explicitly recognizes the synthetic data, single-token analysis, final-token intervention, and Logit Lens approximations.
weaknesses: There is a sign inconsistency in the intervention formulation. Equations (4)-(5) imply that positive λ boosts counterfactual image attention and suppresses factual text attention, whereas Figure 4 and its caption describe the opposite direction. The statement that t_fact moves from rank 3 at λ=0 to rank 31 at λ=3 also appears reversed. This is likely a notation error, but it must be corrected because the equations are needed for reproduction.

Head selection and evaluation appear to use the same examples. The top 20 heads, and possibly intervention/ablation thresholds, are chosen on WHOOPS-AHA! without a reported held-out split or external-dataset test. A split where heads are selected on one subset and tested on another, or evaluation on a separate conflict benchmark, would reduce selection-bias concerns.

The causal evidence is concentrated on attention heads. The claimed functional division between late attention heads and factual MLP blocks is derived mainly from Logit Lens and is not tested through MLP ablation, activation patching, or other causal interventions.

Logit Lens is an approximate decoder that can distort intermediate representations. Although this limitation is acknowledged, head rankings and block-level conclusions depend heavily on it; validation with tuned lenses, alternative decoding probes, or direct activation patching would strengthen the mechanistic claims.

The post-softmax attention intervention is artificial and changes broad image-versus-text information flow rather than precisely editing a conflict mechanism. The KL-divergence and caption-quality results also show that larger interventions substantially alter the output distribution, so the results demonstrate controllability more than they identify the exclusive natural pathway.

External validity is limited. The study uses only two decoder-only VLM families, 500 synthetic/curated WHOOPS images, GPT-4o-generated candidates, and a single next-token decision. It does not establish that the findings generalize to natural conflict images, full multi-token generations, BLIP-style models, or encoder-decoder architectures.

The model-specific filtering of examples and reliance on GPT-4o labels may reduce benchmark independence. More annotation detail is needed, including the number of manual verifiers, disagreement resolution, inter-annotator agreement, and exact checkpoint versions.

The attribution comparison is relatively narrow: the main baseline is vanilla gradient magnitude plus random patches. Comparisons with attention rollout, integrated gradients, Grad-CAM, cross-attention attribution, or other VLM explanation methods would make the claim of superior attribution precision more convincing.

Uncertainty estimates and significance tests are largely absent for the head-localization, intervention, and ablation results. Bootstrap confidence intervals or paired statistical tests would be appropriate, especially for differences between attention and gradient methods.

Conceptually, the work closely extends the mechanistic competition framework of Ortu et al. from language models to VLMs, and concurrent work also studies visual-prior steering. The multimodal dataset and patch-level analysis are valuable, but the broader conceptual novelty is moderate.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: understanding how vision-language models arbitrate between parametric factual knowledge and contradictory visual evidence.
It introduces a controlled resource, WHOOPS-AHA!, pairing counterfactual images with manually verified factual and visually grounded continuation tokens, which is well suited to mechanistic analysis.

The investigation combines complementary levels of evidence: block- and head-level Logit Lens analysis, modality-specific attention measurements, targeted head interventions, and image-patch ablations.

Key patterns are replicated across two substantially different VLMs, LLaVA-NeXT-7b and Gemma3-12b, and the intervention includes random-head controls, head-count sweeps, and analysis of generation degradation.

The patch-ablation and qualitative results provide convincing evidence that counterfactual predictions depend heavily on localized, semantically meaningful anomalous image regions rather than uniformly on the image.
The paper is generally clearly written, and reproducibility is supported by model names, compute requirements, dataset prompts, a stated license, and a commitment to release code and data.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is narrow: the dataset contains only 500 synthetic, curated images, with 436/432 examples after filtering, and the main analysis reduces generation to competition between two selected tokens. This limits conclusions about naturalistic generations and VLMs generally.

The evaluation pipeline risks selection bias because candidate tokens, conflict examples, important heads, and intervention results are all derived from the same dataset. No held-out split, cross-validation, or cross-dataset head-transfer experiment is reported.

The choice of t_cofa using the multimodal model while t_fact is selected from the text-only condition may further inflate the measured visual-override effect. The annotation process also lacks details such as annotator instructions beyond prompts, number of reviewers, and agreement statistics.

Head localization depends strongly on the Logit Lens, an approximate decoding proxy known to introduce projection distortions. Robustness checks with alternative lenses, patchscoping, or direct activation measurements would strengthen the claims.

The intervention scales post-softmax attention rows separately for image and text tokens without renormalization, which changes both information routing and attention-output magnitude. Random-head controls are useful but do not fully exclude norm or off-distribution effects; renormalized interventions, depth/attention-matched controls, and head ablations would be more convincing.

The results demonstrate that selected heads can steer predictions, but they do not establish that these heads uniquely mediate the conflict. Necessity tests such as knockout or activation patching are absent, and contributions from MLPs and the visual encoder are not causally isolated.
The claim that visual information travels directly to the final token with limited intermediate processing is inferred mainly from late-layer attention rather than from path-specific causal tracing.

The comparison against gradient attribution is limited to a Bearer [REDACTED] baseline and is presented mostly through curves without AUC summaries, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Zero-embedding patch ablation is also somewhat out of distribution, so the broad claim of superior attribution precision should be qualified.

Only two decoder-only models in the 7B–12B range are studied, leaving generalization to larger models, encoder-decoder architectures, different visual encoders, and natural free-form generation unresolved.

Although the limitations section acknowledges several of these issues, the paper sometimes phrases its findings as general mechanisms of VLM conflict resolution when the evidence supports a more bounded conclusion for the analyzed synthetic benchmark and models.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important question in multimodal interpretability: how vision-language models resolve conflicts between parametric commonsense knowledge and counterfactual visual evidence.

WHOOPS-AHA is a valuable controlled resource, pairing visually anomalous images with completion prompts and separate factual/counterfactual candidate sets. Its construction, filtering, manual verification, and release details make it useful beyond the present study.

The evidence is organized at multiple levels: block-level Logit Lens analysis, localization to individual attention heads, modality-specific attention patterns, causal intervention, and image-region ablation.

The bidirectional head interventions provide strong causal evidence. Factual accuracy rises substantially from 22% to 74% for LLaVA-NeXT and from 18% to 83% for Gemma3, while reversing the intervention reduces accuracy to about 16%; random-head controls support specificity.

Region-level ablation shows that patches selected by conflict-head attention recover factual predictions more effectively than gradient-selected or randomly selected patches, and qualitative examples align with semantically anomalous objects.

The paper is clearly written, with informative figures and useful appendices covering prompts, generation quality, KL divergence, additional model results, and control experiments. The reported hardware, software, compute budget, and licensing also support reproducibility.
weaknesses: There is a sign inconsistency between equations (4)-(5) and Figure 4. As written, positive lambda boosts image attention in counterfactual heads and suppresses text attention in factual heads, whereas the figure and caption state that positive lambda increases factual accuracy. The exact implementation, sign convention, and any post-scaling renormalization must be clarified.

Head selection, choice of the top 20 heads, and intervention evaluation are performed on the same dataset. A held-out item split, cross-validation, or replication on an external conflict benchmark would reduce concerns about circular selection and would show that the identified heads generalize beyond these candidate pairs.

The core behavioral measure is a pairwise comparison between one factual and one counterfactual next token using Logit Lens. This is a useful controlled proxy, but it does not directly establish that those tokens are the model's free-form answer; Logit Lens projections and single-token continuation are also known approximations.

The claim of superior attribution precision is mainly supported by ablation curves rather than overlap with human-annotated anomaly regions. Zeroing visual embeddings can also create out-of-distribution inputs, and several results lack confidence intervals or significance tests.

Generalizability is limited to two decoder-only VLMs and to synthetic, curated WHOOPS images. Replication on naturalistic conflicts or additional architectures would strengthen the generality of the proposed factual/counterfactual head distinction.

The intervention targets only the final token position and attention heads. Causal contributions from MLPs, visual encoders, and earlier token positions are not directly tested, despite the paper's broader claims about the model's conflict-resolution machinery.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem for multimodal NLP: how vision-language models resolve conflicts between parametric knowledge and contradictory visual evidence.
The paper is clearly written and well organized, with an informative overview figure, explicit definitions of factual versus counterfactual predictions, and detailed appendices.
WHOOPS-AHA provides a useful token-level benchmark for controlled multimodal conflict analysis, including paired factual and visually grounded continuations.
The empirical analysis is multi-pronged, combining Logit Lens inspection, block- and head-level measurements, attention-mass comparisons, intervention, patch ablation, and random-head controls.

The authors include meaningful robustness checks, including evaluation on Visual CounterFact, overlap of identified heads across datasets, and POPE tests showing that the heads are not merely generic visual-processing components.
Reproducibility is supported by released data, prompts in the appendices, public model implementations, hardware details, and a report of total compute.
weaknesses: The central attention-head intervention is not sufficiently controlled. The post-softmax attention weights are rescaled without renormalization, and for λ > 1 the factor 1−λ becomes negative, reaching −2 at λ = 3, while other weights are scaled up to 4. This changes total attention mass and introduces out-of-distribution negative attention, so the large output changes may partly reflect intervention artifacts.

The intervention simultaneously modifies counterfactual heads' image attention and factual heads' text attention. This bidirectional design does not isolate the causal contribution of either group; separate or factorial interventions are needed.

Evidence for the identified circuit relies heavily on the Logit Lens, which is an approximate diagnostic rather than an exact decoding proxy. Individual-head projections and final-token measurements are suggestive, but they do not by themselves establish a complete conflict-resolution mechanism.

Dataset validation depends primarily on LLM judges. Human validation covers only 20 examples, exact agreement is modest for alignment, and inter-annotator agreement is not clearly reported. Because the examples and candidate tokens are GPT-generated and derived from the existing WHOOPS! images, broader independent validation would strengthen the resource.

The main behavioral metric is largely a forced single-token comparison between one factual and one counterfactual token rather than analysis of unrestricted generation, which may not fully demonstrate real-world hallucination behavior.

The claim that attention attribution is more precise than gradient-based attribution is based on only 20 images, two models, SAM-derived masks, and one attribution metric; the evidence is promising but not sufficient for a broad superiority claim.

Some mechanistic interpretations are overstated. Attention at the final token does not prove that visual information bypasses intermediate processing, and the limited MLP intervention on only the last three blocks does not establish a definitive attention–MLP dissociation.

Generalization is restricted to two open-weight, late-fusion decoder-style VLMs and a relatively simple color-conflict dataset, limiting claims about other fusion architectures and more realistic knowledge conflicts.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: how VLMs resolve conflicts between parametric commonsense knowledge and misleading visual evidence. The introduced WHOOPS-AHA! dataset is purpose-built for mechanistic analysis, with controlled counterfactual images, paired factual and counterfactual continuations, explicit construction requirements, filtering, and validation.

The empirical methodology is unusually thorough. It combines Logit Lens inspection, head-level localization, bidirectional interventions, random-head controls, MLP interventions, patch ablation, gradient-based comparisons, SAM-based quantitative attribution, a POPE specificity test, and replication on an independently constructed Visual CounterFact dataset.

The causal evidence goes beyond correlational attention visualization. Targeted interventions substantially and bidirectionally shift model behavior, while randomly selected heads produce negligible changes and MLP interventions are much weaker. Patch ablations further support the claim that the identified heads attend to semantically relevant counterfactual regions.

The main findings are consistent across two different VLMs, LLaVA-NeXT-7B and Gemma3-12B: conflict-related signals are concentrated in upper-layer attention heads, counterfactual heads attend more strongly to image tokens, and factual heads are more aligned with internal knowledge. The cross-dataset head overlap also strengthens the transferability claim.

The paper is clearly written, with informative figures and extensive appendices covering dataset prompts, validation, intervention parameters, controls, and additional model analyses. Compute requirements, model implementations, and dataset/code release intentions also support reproducibility.
weaknesses: External validity is limited. The conclusions are demonstrated on two late-fusion, attention-centric, open-weight models and do not necessarily generalize to early- or mid-fusion architectures, encoder-decoder VLMs, proprietary models, or much larger systems.

Head discovery and evaluation are not fully separated. The top factual and counterfactual heads are selected using the same conflict setting in which their causal effects are then measured. The random-head controls and Visual CounterFact replication mitigate this concern, but a held-out head-discovery split would make the claim cleaner.

Logit Lens is an approximate diagnostic rather than a direct reading of model computation. The focus on one highest-probability factual and one counterfactual token, drawn from small generated candidate sets, simplifies free-form generation and may not fully capture how conflicts are resolved in longer, more ambiguous outputs.

The attention intervention is causally informative but not a minimal circuit intervention. It simultaneously changes attention weights for particular head groups and modalities, and rescaling post-softmax attention can alter both information routing and activation magnitude. Additional activation patching or factorial modality/head controls would strengthen the mechanistic interpretation.

Dataset construction and quality assessment rely heavily on GPT-4o-generated captions and tokens plus LLM-as-a-judge validation. Human evaluation covers only a 20-item subset, and exact human-judge agreement is modest for some categories, so annotation or candidate-selection bias remains possible.

Although the implicit commonsense-conflict setting is valuable, the paper is close to several concurrent 2025 studies on modality-preference heads, steering vectors, and hallucination heads. A more direct empirical comparison with these methods, rather than a mostly conceptual differentiation, would better clarify the incremental contribution.

Some of the main intervention and localization plots do not report uncertainty estimates or robustness across multiple prompt formulations. The effects are large and consistent, but additional statistical reporting would increase confidence in their stability.
